strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates a genuine theoretical limitation of CSCNNs (incompleteness of the steerable kernel basis for O(2,0)), with a concrete worked example (Example 3.2, Appendix A.4) showing why single-layer CSCNNs cannot express angular frequency-2 components

The proposed fix is elegant and well-grounded: conditioning the implicit kernel on equivariantly pooled input features extends the kernel network input, and the steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.1) and its satisfaction via Clifford-equivariant implicit parameterization (Lemma 4.2, Prop. 4.1) are proven cleanly in the appendix

The implicit parameterization approach neatly avoids the practical infeasibility of solving the steerability constraint per conditioning value, and the use of a translation-invariant conditioning operator (mean pooling) preserves template-matching efficiency at negligible extra cost

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four PDE benchmarks (NS, SWE-1, SWE-5, MW3, relativistic MW2) with 14 baselines, parameter-matched comparisons (except SWE-5), data-efficiency curves, a scaling study on SWE-5, and a numerical equivariance error check (Table 2) confirming the theory

Honesty about theoretical limits: the completeness claim is presented as an explicit conjecture (Conjecture 4.1) rather than an overreaching theorem, and the difficulty of proving it is candidly discussed; empirical validation including a novel relativistic Maxwell (R^{1,2}) dataset is a useful contribution
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is left unproven: the title and abstract advertise a 'Complete Kernel Basis', but completeness is only stated as a conjecture and validated by a single sympy-verified O(2,0) example (Appendices A.4-A.5) plus indirect empirical evidence; the title therefore overstates what is established

The practical conditioning mechanism (global mean pooling with circular masking) is a coarse mean-field approximation; the paper does not characterize how much expressivity is lost relative to general conditioning (Eq. 10), and ablations over alternative conditioning operators (max/learnable pooling, finer conditioning regions) are deferred to future work

Equivariance is only empirically verified for E(2) (Table 2); no numerical equivariance validation is reported for the pseudo-Euclidean/Minkowski setting (MW2), which is a key selling point of the Clifford framework

In the SWE-5 scaling comparison, baseline results are taken from prior work without parameter matching and with mixed assumptions (different model sizes), weakening the 'on par with SOTA' claim; e.g., C-CSCNN (55M, 2.94%) still trails CViT-L (92M, 1.56%)

The mechanism behind the performance gains is not fully disentangled: gains could stem from added nonlinearity/global context rather than kernel-basis completeness per se; no ablation isolates the frequency-2 component contribution

Reproducibility support is thin: no code release is mentioned, no explicit limitations/reproducibility statement, and the appendix contains several incomplete or erroneous sentences (e.g., 'trained on one node of', 'The dataset os obtained', 'it the part', 'SW2-1') that suggest insufficient proofreading

The equivariance-preserving circular masking addresses corner artifacts only in the continuum limit; the practical impact of remaining discretization-induced equivariance error on results is not quantified

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly articulates a genuine, previously unreported limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (incompleteness of the implicit kernel basis, e.g. missing frequency-2 components for O(2,0)), and traces the source of the problem to the input type of the kernel network (Example 3.2).

The theoretical development is sound: the steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.1), the equivariance of Clifford-steerable conditional kernels (Lemma 4.2), and the equivariance condition on the conditioning operator T (Proposition 4.1) are stated precisely and proofs in Appendix A are correct and self-contained.
The incompleteness argument (Appendix A.4) and the partial completeness argument (A.5) are backed by symbolic verification with sympy, which is a nice concrete validation of the algebraic claims.
The conjecture in Section 4.4 is honestly labeled as a conjecture rather than a theorem, with a frank discussion of why proving it is hard.

Experiments are reasonably broad (four PDE benchmarks, ~15 baselines, parameter matching in most settings), and the empirical gains over the original CSCNN are large (33-54% error reductions). The equivariance error check (Table 2) supports the theoretical claims experimentally.
The circular masking trick for restoring O(n)-equivariance of pooled statistics on square grids (Appendix B) is a practical and clearly explained detail.
weaknesses: The central claim advertised in the title ('Complete Kernel Basis') is never proven: completeness of the conditional kernel basis remains Conjecture 4.1, validated only empirically. Example 4.1 shows only that frequency-2 components *can* be represented, not that the basis spans the full analytical solution space; a direct kernel-space expressivity experiment (e.g., fitting analytical basis functions) would have substantially strengthened the case.

The methodological novelty is incremental. Conditioning implicit kernels on derived features is a natural extension of Zhdanov et al. (2023, 2024), and the specific conditioning operator used is global mean pooling, i.e., a mean-field approximation. The claim that this is 'strictly more expressive than a standard convolution' is asserted, not proven.

The scaling narrative overstates the SWE-5 results: C-CSCNN (55M, 2.94%) is in fact clearly beaten by CViT-L (92M, 1.56%), and CViT-B (30M, 2.69%) also edges out the 55M C-CSCNN. 'Perform on par with leading approaches' is a generous characterization; the honest conclusion is that the method is competitive in the small-parameter regime.

Key results are presented only as plots without numerical values, seeds, or error bars (Figures 2 and 3), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the data-efficiency comparisons; some comparisons omit baselines that were introduced in the setup (e.g., FNO/G-FNO relegated to a thin appendix table).

The conditioning on a single globally pooled multivector means every kernel in the network depends on the entire input field; the paper gives little analysis of the practical or theoretical implications of this non-locality (e.g., behavior under distribution shift between train/test global statistics).

Reproducibility is limited: no code or dataset release is mentioned (the new relativistic Maxwell dataset is described but no availability statement is given), and several writing errors undermine polish ('evalution', 'os obtained', 'utilisied', 'SW2-1', the truncated sentence 'trained on one node of with 1-4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs', inconsistent Table/Figure numbering for the FNO results).

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly diagnoses a genuine theoretical limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (incompleteness of the kernel basis, illustrated concretely via Example 3.2 for O(2,0)), which is a valuable contribution to the equivariant deep learning literature in its own right.

The theoretical development is sound: the steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.1), the equivariance of the composition H∘K̂ (Lemma 4.2), and the requirement of equivariance of the conditioning operator T (Proposition 4.1) are all proven in the appendix, and the equivariance claims are additionally validated numerically (Table 2, relative errors ~1e-7).

The template-matching formulation (conditioning on a global translation-invariant field via mean pooling) is a sensible and well-motivated trade-off between expressivity and computational efficiency, and it preserves parameter sharing so the overhead is negligible.

Empirical evaluation is broad: four PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water 1-step and 5-step, 3D Maxwell, relativistic 2+1D Maxwell), comparisons against 14 baselines including state-of-the-art neural solvers (Transolver, CViT, LSM), data-efficiency scaling curves, and a model-scaling study (Table 1) showing strong results at small parameter counts (10M C-CSCNN beats CViT-B).

The paper is honest about the completeness claim, framing it as a conjecture (Conjecture 4.1) rather than overclaiming a theorem, and gives a reasonable explanation of why a full proof is non-trivial.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: implementation details (architecture, hyperparameters, conditioning implementation with circular masking), dataset construction, and hardware are described; the incompleteness/completeness arguments are supported by symbolic computation snippets (Codes 1–3).
weaknesses: The central completeness claim (Conjecture 4.1) is left unproven; the formal result is only verified for O(2,0) at the level of a single geometric product and empirically. The title and abstract's framing ('Complete Kernel Basis') is stronger than what is actually established.

The method's expressivity gain rests on a mean-field conditioning operator (global mean pooling), which is acknowledged to be a crude approximation of the fully general conditional convolution of Definition 4.1. No alternatives (e.g., learnable or regional pooling) are ablated, so the practical expressivity-performance trade-off space is unexplored.

Originality is moderate: input-conditioned/nonlinear convolution kernels are well established (message passing, continuous-kernel networks, Nyholm et al. 2025 non-linear equivariant maps), and the work is a fairly direct extension of the implicit parameterization of Zhdanov et al. (2023) into the Clifford setting of Zhdanov et al. (2024).

Several experimental comparisons are uneven: SWE-5 baselines are taken from Wang et al. (2025) rather than retrained under matched conditions; FNO/G-FNO results are relegated to an appendix table with missing entries (e.g., G-FNO absent for Maxwell); and in the data-efficiency experiments the comparison is mostly against architecturally similar ResNet variants rather than the full set of strong baselines.

The choice of T (what exactly is pooled, which channels/grades) and its sensitivity is not ablated; the conditioning mechanism risks reducing to a global scaling heuristic whose benefit may not generalize beyond the tested benchmarks.

Presentation has notable sloppiness: typos ('evalution', 'dataset os obtained', 'and and'), Code 3 prints kx[0] where k[0] appears intended, an inconsistent 'Table 6'/'Figure 6' reference, 'SW2-1' vs 'SWE-1' naming, and the phrase 'training on one node of' with a missing facility name. There is no explicit limitations section, and the conditioning multivector's dependence on the (non-compact) global average raises stability questions that are only briefly addressed (grade-wise normalization, needed for MW2).

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated technical deficiency in CSCNNs (incompleteness of the implicit kernel basis, demonstrated for O(2,0) against the analytical solution of Weiler & Cesa 2019) and proposes a principled fix: conditioning the kernel on an equivariantly pooled auxiliary multivector derived from the input field.

The theory is developed carefully: the steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.2), the equivariance of the Clifford-steerable conditional kernel construction (Lemma 4.3), and the required equivariance of the conditioning operator T (Proposition 4.5) are all proven in the appendix, with sympy-verified algebraic examples (Codes 1-3) substantiating both the incompleteness and the recovery of angular frequency components.

The efficiency trade-off is handled thoughtfully: the translation-invariant conditioning operator T enables template matching (parameter sharing), and the empirical overhead is negligible (~0.87% inference time vs. CSCNN).

Experimental evaluation is broad and reasonably fair: four PDE tasks including a genuinely pseudo-Euclidean relativistic Maxwell setting, ~15 baselines with parameter matching, data-efficiency sweeps, scaling results (SWE-5), an equivariance-error measurement (10^-7 order, matching theory), and an ablation of conditioning operators including a non-equivariant random condition, which isolates the benefit of equivariant conditioning.

The limitations section is honest and specific: completeness for general O(p,q) is explicitly stated as an unproven conjecture rather than oversold, and constraints of the multivector field-type assumption are acknowledged.
Implementation details (architecture, training, datasets, circular masking for grid equivariance, JAX/Flax) are documented sufficiently to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim - completeness of the conditional kernel basis for general O(p,q) - remains an unproven conjecture. Only the O(2,0) case is demonstrated, and the supporting evidence (Appendix A.5, Code 3) is informal and partially truncated, so the headline theoretical contribution is empirically but not formally established.

The novelty is incremental relative to prior work: conditioning kernels on input-derived features is standard in message passing / point convolutions, and the contribution is essentially adapting this idea to the Clifford-steerable setting plus the associated constraint derivations. The derived results are natural consequences of existing implicit parameterization theory (Zhdanov et al., 2023).

Mean pooling produces a single global mean-field condition, which is a very coarse form of conditioning. The observed performance gains may stem from the added input-dependence (nonlinearity) rather than specifically restoring the claimed missing kernel basis; the ablation does not fully disentangle these effects, and more expressive conditioning operators are deferred to future work.

Against state-of-the-art baselines the results are mixed: C-CSCNN is second-best on both electrodynamics tasks (behind Transolver) and on SWE-5 (behind CViT-L at a smaller parameter count of 92M vs. 55M). The strongest claims hold mainly for fluid dynamics tasks and against the original CSCNN.

Presentation has noticeable sloppiness: typos ('The dataset os obtained', 'utilisied', 'organized by the what capabilities'), leftover variables in Eq. 37 of the proof of Proposition 4.5 ('x, y' are not in scope of that argument), and minor notational inconsistencies, which reduces polish though not correctness.
Only a single-layer equivariance check is reported; end-to-end model equivariance and sensitivity of results to the conditioning operator choice across tasks (beyond SWE-1) are not evaluated.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated weakness of CSCNNs (Zhdanov et al., 2024): the implicit kernel basis is incomplete for vector-vector interactions (missing frequency-2 components), demonstrated clearly for O(2,0) with analytical worked examples (Example 3.6, Appendix A.4-A.5).

The proposed fix is simple and well-integrated: conditioning the Clifford-steerable implicit kernel on an equivariant statistic of the input field (mean pooling) restores higher-frequency components at negligible computational cost (0.87% slower per Table 5).

The experimental evaluation is fairly thorough: four PDE benchmarks, 15 baselines with matched parameter counts, data-efficiency curves (Figure 2), a scaling study on SWE-5 (Table 2), a conditioning-operator ablation (Table 3), and an empirical equivariance check (Eq. 18) showing error of the same order as the unconditioned model (~3.4e-7).

The paper honestly labels the general completeness claim as a conjecture (Conjecture 4.7), leaves its proof to future work, and includes a candid limitations section covering conditioning-operator simplicity, discretization-induced equivariance error, and inherited multivector-representation restrictions.
The improvement over the CSCNN baseline is consistent and substantial (e.g., -33.9% to -54.1% MSE per Figure 1c), and C-CSCNN is the best model on the fluid dynamics tasks (NS, SWE-1) in Table 1.
weaknesses: There is a logical gap in the central theoretical result. The proof of Proposition 4.5 (Appendix A.3) asserts that Eqs. 35-36 coincide 'if and only if' ρ(g)T[f] = T[ρ(g)f] (Eq. 38). This requires that the kernel network K̂ is injective in its conditioning argument, which is never established; a network can map distinct inputs to the same output, so the claimed iff does not follow. Since Lemma 4.2's steerability constraint must hold for all feature fields, this gap undermines the equivariance guarantee as stated and needs repair or a careful reformulation.

The headline theoretical contribution, completeness of the conditional kernel basis, is not actually proven. Section 4.4 only demonstrates that frequency-2 components become representable for O(2,0) (Example 4.6), yet the Limitations section claims 'we prove completeness for O(2,0)' — inconsistent with the body, which explicitly formulates Conjecture 4.7 and defers the proof. The central claim motivating the paper is therefore conjectural, supported only by empirics.

The contribution is incremental relative to prior work: conditional/input-dependent equivariant kernels are well studied (message passing, point convolutions, and non-linear equivariant maps per Nyholm et al., 2025, which the authors cite), and the conditioning operator actually used is plain masked mean pooling — a global mean-field that the paper itself concedes is 'less expressive'. The gap between the general framework (arbitrary conditioning) and what is validated (mean pooling) limits the significance of the empirical findings.

The method does not surpass the state of the art: Transolver outperforms C-CSCNN on both electrodynamics tasks (MW3, MW2) at every dataset size (Table 1), and on SWE-5 the 55M C-CSCNN trails CViT-S (13M) and CViT-B (30M) (Table 2), i.e., the equivariant model is less parameter-efficient than the attention baseline it is compared against. The SWE-5 comparison also mixes parameter counts inconsistently with the other tasks.

The incompleteness/incompleteness-fix analysis is carried out only for O(2,0), while experiments span O(2), O(3) and O(1,2); no comparable kernel-basis analysis is given for the other symmetry groups, so the mechanism behind the observed gains outside 2D Euclidean data is not established.

Presentation issues: proof-of-concept claims are supported by sympy printouts (Codes 1-3) rather than formal statements, Appendix A.3 contains a degenerate comparison (Eq. 37 equates identical left-hand sides), and there are multiple typos/grammatical errors (e.g., 'evaluation' → 'evalution', 'it is the part that is missing', 'os obtained', 'utilisationed') suggesting insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper identifies and rigorously diagnoses a genuine limitation of prior work: it demonstrates (Example 3.6, Appendix A.4, verified symbolically with sympy) that the implicit Clifford-steerable kernel basis of Zhdanov et al. (2024) misses the frequency-2 angular component for O(2,0), which explains the limited expressivity of standard CSCNNs.

The theoretical treatment is careful: the steerability constraint for input-dependent kernels is derived (Lemma 4.2 with a correct-looking proof), the composition of an equivariant conditioning operator T with an equivariant implicit kernel is shown to preserve E(p,q)-equivariance (Prop 4.5, Cor. 4.4), and the O(2,0) completeness recovery is demonstrated (Example 4.6, Appendix A.5). Claims that are not proven (Conjecture 4.7 for general O(p,q)) are honestly labeled as conjectures.

The proposed fix is simple and essentially free computationally: conditioning the kernel network on a translation-invariant pooled multivector adds only ~0.87% inference overhead over CSCNN (Table 5), yet yields large gains (e.g., -53.7% MSE on NS, -54.1% on SWE relative to CSCNN).

Empirical evaluation is broad and largely fair: four PDE benchmarks (NS, SWE-1/5, 3D Maxwell, relativistic 2+1D Maxwell), ~15 baselines including recent SOTA (Transolver, CViT, LSM, G-FNO), parameter-matched comparisons for most tasks, scaling analysis on SWE-5, an ablation of conditioning operators (mean vs. max vs. random), and a numerical equivariance-error verification (~3.4e-7, comparable to the unconditioned baseline).
The limitations section is candid: the general completeness conjecture is open, only simple conditioning operators were explored, and discretization breaks exact equivariance in practice.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is only partially established: completeness of the conditional kernel basis is proven only for O(2,0); for the general O(p,q) case it remains a conjecture validated 'empirically'. Readers cannot know whether the expressivity gap is closed in the settings (e.g., Lorentz group R^{1,2}) that are most distinctive for Clifford methods.

The chosen conditioning operator (global mean pooling) is a mean-field approximation: the kernel is modulated by the same global context everywhere, so the operator, while non-linear, has limited spatial adaptivity. This plausibly explains why C-CSCNNs remain behind Transolver on the electrodynamics tasks (MW2, MW3), and the paper's ablation only compares pooling variants and a random condition—not richer equivariant conditioning (e.g., local/patch pooling, learned pooling), which the authors defer to future work.

The empirical contribution is strongest relative to the CSCNN baseline it directly extends; against the broader SOTA the results are 'on par' rather than clearly superior (best on NS/SWE-1, second on MW2/MW3, and behind CViT-L/U-F2Net on SWE-5), so the practical significance beyond the CSCNN lineage is modest.
The SWE-5 comparison is not parameter-matched and mixes baselines taken from prior papers, weakening the comparability of the scaling claims.

Some minor presentation issues (typos such as 'evalution', 'it is the part that is missing', inconsistent significance digits in Table 1), and Figure 2 shows only C-CSCNN vs. CSCNN rather than including the strongest baselines.
